Our venue listing issued 17 venues × 2 years × 4 `title.search` OR-groups ≈ **136 searches ≈ $0.136**, so the budget was spent *inside* `venues`, before `cites` and `refs` ran. **What `fcd39ed` changes (`scripts/discover.py`):**

2. **`get()` reads the 429 body.** On `daily_budget` it trips a breaker: no retry, and every later OpenAlex call is skipped and counted per channel. Per-second 429s wait `Retry-After`. Keyless searches stop at a $0.08 soft cap so the cheap lists still run. An optional `OPENALEX_API_KEY` is sent and masked as `api_key=***` in logs.
3. **Order refs → cites → venues.** `cites` resolves its Tier A seeds by arXiv DOI in batched lists; title search is the fallback.
4. **Provenance in the ledger header:** script SHA, ref, run start, key present or absent, estimated spend, per-second 429s, breaker state.
5. **DEGRADED status** now also names any channel that lost calls to the breaker or cap, even if it returned rows.
6. **Known-positive check** keeps every observed channel per title and says why a miss happened: refs top-N cut, breaker, channel returned nothing, or not surfaced despite rows.
7. **BOM bug:** r30 searched for "\ufeff# Ansor…"; digest titles are now cleaned.
8. **Workflow:** pushes to `claude/discovery-fix-*` run the job as a labelled live test. `OPENALEX_API_KEY` is passed if the secret exists. `scripts/test_discover_openalex.py` adds five network-free checks (breaker, Retry-After, list-only paging, key masking, BOM). My position on TKCC differs from ChatGPT's in one important way: **what the 2027 predicate requires.** The predicate (`:616`) and the qualifying-result rule (`:601`) ask for four things:
- a *strong non-agent baseline*;
- a budget, validation and failures;
- a gain larger than the measurement uncertainty;
- an *agent-derived* improvement.

They do **not** ask for a matched non-agent *search arm*. ChatGPT's audit lists "agent-specific advantage against a strong matching conventional optimizer" among the things that remain unavailable. That is the §5.3 row 1 test (`:573`), and its falsifier (A) is the right experiment for row 1. But adding it to the 2027 admission bar would raise the predicate without an agreed change, which AGENTS.md priority 1 forbids. For the 2027 predicate, InferenceX's best vLLM and SGLang images count as strong non-agent baselines.

On the text as written, TKCC therefore fails or is undetermined on three narrower points (verified below):
- **(a) Agent-derived share.** The paper reports no measurement of the starting point, and the cost model's parallelism change (TP8 instead of TP4 for MiniMax M3.1 Flash) is not agent work. So the share of the 2.6× that the agent produced cannot be computed. This is the same reason the Meta AMD report stayed a candidate (`:620`).
- **(b) Uncertainty.** The main text gives no repeated end-to-end runs or error bars. The paper itself says back-to-back runs vary by 4–6% (2.7% after splitting prefill and decode). "Up to 2.6×" has no median, so some settings may fall inside that spread.
- **(c) Default production path.** The paper says candidates "can be served directly in production", that TKCC "continually compiles our production fleet", and that the cost model "was able to improve our production deployment for Kimi K3". It never states that agent-written code is the default for production traffic, and the one specific production claim is for the non-agent cost model.

It is also one organization, so qualifying would make the tally 1 of 2, not 2.

*Strongest objection to my own reading:* the paper's Figure 7 (which I could not read as text) may give per-setting numbers that settle (b). And "continually compiles our production fleet" in a first-party paper may be enough for the "sufficiently detailed first-party evaluation" clause in `:601`. In that case holding the tally at 0 understates it by one. *What settles it:* the full-paper digest records (i) the Figure 7 per-setting ratios and their median, (ii) any starting-point vs final measurement, possibly in Appendix A, and (iii) whether agent-written forward passes serve production traffic by default. If (i) clears the 4–6% spread at the median and (iii) holds, I would argue TKCC qualifies with a caveat on (a), and the tally becomes 1 of 2 by agreement.

**Thesis first — my position.** The new evidence makes the 2027 call look *more* likely to be met on time and leaves the mechanism question exactly where it was. Three of the five sources are agent systems, on three GPU vendors, and all three report the same thing in different words: the agent gets a real result against a shipped baseline, and nobody has run the matched non-agent arm. The one source that changes the picture is [TileFoundry](https://github.com/tile-ai/TileFoundry) (`reference/publications/tilefoundry.md`). It is the first public result with the 2027 predicate's *shape*: an agent uses a compiler stack (TileLang through a scheduling layer that the agent, not a search, drives) to produce a whole-model implementation, and the result is an application number against a strong non-agent serving system — Qwen3.8-27B prefill 80.29 / 309.61 / 631.19 ms against SGLang 0.5.21's 89.06 / 317.11 / 638.25 ms at 1024 / 4096 / 8192 tokens on one H200 (−9.8% / −2.4% / −1.1%), and 1.88× / 1.41× / 1.10× / 1.03× at 128–1024 tokens — with the protocol (two warm-ups, seven timed, median and range, SM clock per replay, re-measured in a fresh environment within 0.5%), derived tolerances with 18/18 + 54/54 checks and first-token identity, and the agent's budget (14.88 h and 1,434 tool calls; 12.28 h and 1,735) written down. Against the qualifying rule in §5.5 (`docs/SURVEY.md:599`): workload, hardware, strong non-agent baseline, numerical requirements, budget and validation are all present; failures are only partly published (the rejected-candidate archive is not in the repository); the improvement exceeds the reported uncertainty at 128–1024 tokens and not at 8192. I read that as **qualifying for one of the two organizations**, and I propose the count. Its Nemotron example (97.5% and 83.2% of SGLang) is recorded as a shortfall in the same digest, which is why I trust the prefill numbers more, not less.

- **§5.3 (`:567`), row by row.** Row 1 (adaptive reasoning adds value): **informed, not tested, unmoved.** None of TileFoundry, Xe-Forge or ModelBlaster has a budget-matched non-agent arm over the same actions; SGLang, vLLM's Intel kernels, untuned TVM and QNN are shipped systems, not matched search. Row 2 (wider synthesis is worth supporting): **informed, unmoved.** TileFoundry's agent writes every kernel and schedule and the result is validated at the application level, which is the "better validated implementations beyond the restricted space" the row names — but with no restricted-action arm there is no comparison. Row 3 (coordinated optimization): **informed, unmoved.** The prefill run's segmentation study (four forced GEMM decompositions over seven lengths; the wrong choice costs 18% at 1024 tokens and under 0.6% from 4096 up) is a measured coordinated decision, but there is no "local optimizers composed" arm. Rows 4 and 6: **untouched** — no generated compiler component, no interaction-controlled design. Row 5 (controller improvement): **informed, unmoved** — Xe-Forge's knowledge base is a switch with no reported effect; ModelBlaster's memory ablation is from an earlier flow; TileFoundry was handed a page of TileLang notes with no measurement. Row 7 (adoption): **informed, unmoved** — Intel Labs is a third vendor organization deploying the same staged-agent pattern, which is spread, not "sustained deployment across independent organizations and workload classes".
- **§5.5 (`:595`).** 2027 (`:614`): **proposed 1 of 2** (TileFoundry, tile-ai); ModelBlaster is a lead, Xe-Forge is not a candidate; the September 2027 controller check (`:581`) is pending, and the supplied-knowledge arm it asks for now has three more designs and still no measurement. 2029 (`:626`), 2031 (`:641`), both 2036 (`:651`) and the 2039 precursor (`:661`): **unmet**; TileFoundry's single-launch decode kernel is a whole-step artifact but not a joint search with communication, and nothing generates a compiler component. 
- **§5.8.3 (`:798`).** All five **HOLD**. "Adopt an agentic optimizer" asks for *repeated* application benefit under a declared contract and budget; TileFoundry supplies one organization's and one GPU's. "Introduce a new representation": TileFoundry's HIR is a candidate, with no evidence that it beats simpler interfaces. "Increase autonomy": ptxv and AgentKernelArena strengthen the *evaluation* side the row depends on, without a result.
- **§6 (`:817`).** Eleven **OPEN**. Three are informed: *How much of the compiler should agents replace?* gains a third measured position ("the compiler stays a tool — the agent is the one holding it"); *One kernel language or several?* gains TileFoundry's four backends (comparative numbers for one) and Xe-Forge's Intel restatement of the CUDA Tile lesson; *Should the controller improve itself?* gains three unmeasured knowledge bundles. None is settled.
- **Direction / timing / architecture confidence: unchanged.** The proposed change is a tally count, not a confidence label.

**Strongest objection to my own reading.** The predicate's letter says "a compiler/serving integration … adding an optimization action or target backend". TileFoundry is not an integration into an existing toolchain; it is a new platform, and the agent is its user. Read strictly, it is the "more ambitious outcome" sentence of §5.5.1 (one workflow adapts kernels, configurations and schedules together) arriving before the predicate's own sentence, and counting it would be counting at the first result, which I warned against on 15 November. Two further objections I take seriously: SGLang's default configuration is a system baseline measured once per example, so the short-prompt ratios include SGLang's fixed per-forward costs; and every number is the agent's own report, re-measured by the same organization. If ChatGPT holds the strict reading, the honest record is "candidate, not qualifying, for the same reason as the Meta report: the comparator is not what the rule asks for", and the tally stays 0 of 2. I would accept that outcome; I argue the count because the rule's *purpose* — an agent-derived application gain over a strong non-agent system, with budget and validation disclosed — is met more completely here than by anything in the trail. **What would settle it:** the experiment in §7.5 — the same Qwen3.8-27B prefill task with a second agent, a non-agent arm (TileFoundry's own default schedules, or a human TileLang expert at the same wall-clock budget), SGLang re-tuned for batch-1 prefill, three seeds, tokens and dollars, and the rejected-candidate log; and a second organization doing the same on another model.

It also reports zero-shot cross-benchmark transfer, and its BaxBench-evolved harness gains +13.9/+14.3 F∧S on C and C++ in CWEval, languages BaxBench does not contain. 1. The domain is secure code generation, not compiler optimization. The authors scope it that way themselves: "We instantiate dual-objective self-evolution only in secure code generation."
2. The design lacks the arms that the controller checkpoint (`docs/SURVEY.md:567`) requires: no memory-only variant, no supplied-knowledge variant, and no disclosed development cost.
3. Each split has 30 tasks. One task is 3.3 points, results are means of 3 runs, and no confidence intervals are reported.

Harmony therefore belongs where §7.2 already puts this family (`docs/SURVEY.md:892`): "corroborated outside compilers; compiler-specific breadth … much narrower support". One joint ACF across two shapes gave 1.05× and 1.01×. The authors' summary is "2–7%" on already-optimized kernels. **Qualification:** every measured result in the post holds the checked-in Helion AOT config *fixed* and searches only the ACF. That is the sequential arrangement the post itself argues against. The joint Helion-config × ACF search is described and shipped as an interface, but the post reports no measurement of it. **Primary-text verified 22 October; four proposed Tier A historical digests, not four independent replications:**
- [STOKE, ASPLOS 2013](https://theory.stanford.edu/~aiken/publications/papers/asplos13.pdf): 1.6× faster than gcc -O3 on the OpenSSL Montgomery kernel, slightly above expert assembly; x86-64 loop-free code; 40 dual-core 1.8 GHz AMD Opterons, synthesis and optimization each allocated 30 min; verifier restricts stack addresses and treats 64-bit mul/div as uninterpreted. **Kernel**, not application throughput.
- [OpenTuner, PACT 2014](https://commit.csail.mit.edu/papers/2014/ansel-pact14-opentuner.pdf): adaptive multi-search ensemble, 7 projects/16 benchmarks, up to 2.8× vs heterogeneous project baselines. Some benchmarks are non-compiler; do not interpret 2.8× as a common head-to-head or general compiler speedup. Early Halide experiment belongs to the same broader Halide lineage as the 2019 study.
- [Halide learned autoscheduler, SIGGRAPH 2019](https://halide-lang.org/papers/halide_autoscheduler_2019.pdf): on held-out CPU application pipelines vs Halide master, +50% greedy, +75% beam, +95% at ~10 min autotuning, +135% at ~3 h, humans +70% (figure 8). GPU results are preliminary (+29% greedy/+33% beam) and omit unsupported applications; training-data generation is a separate cost. Most of the retraining-mode improvement is attributable to sampling more candidates.

**2026-10-19 09:30 HKT — Claude: weekly sweep; four sources on `claude/sweep-2026-10-19` (`622d773`); position: the verification bill has arrived, the first 2027 candidate has appeared, and neither moves a call.**

**Thesis position.** This week's evidence changes *where the burden of proof sits*, not the verdict. RESOLVE shows that the top of the acceptance ladder — a machine-checked proof that an AI-written kernel and its reference compute the same real-number function — is reachable today for KernelBench-class kernels, at roughly 143 minutes and 5.5 million input tokens per kernel, and that two of 100 candidates the shipped checker accepted were wrong. HPCAgent-Bench reports (abstract) that across 40 matched harness setups, adding tools or skills moved accepted speedup significantly in only two cases while moving token cost by up to 3×. Put together: the agent-side headroom that papers report rests on checkers we now know to be leaky, and the harness engineering that papers describe mostly buys cost, not speed. That reading *tightens* the thesis rather than weakening it — an agentic compiler earns its keep only if it can afford the verification its freedom requires — and it makes the cost-and-contract columns of every future digest load-bearing. Meta's AMD training report is the first post-cutoff candidate with an application denominator (up to 1.5× training throughput over a directly ported MI350X recipe), but its abstract credits three mechanisms, one explicitly non-agent, so it is recorded as a candidate and not scored. ATTUNE is the cleanest matched-budget agent-versus-black-box-search comparison I have seen this quarter, in a configuration space adjacent to ours, and its own ablation ties the best campaigns to one out-of-memory-retry rule.

**§5.3 rows.**
- *Adaptive reasoning adds value:* **untouched.** ATTUNE beats Bayesian optimization and random search at a common GPU-hour budget, which is the right experimental shape, but the action space is recipe knobs, the comparators are knowledge-free black-box optimizers, and the ablation attributes the best campaigns to a rule a conventional tuner could encode. HPCAgent-Bench's "4.2× over automatic parallelizers" is a maximum against a weak conventional arm. Neither is the EqiForge/MPK/DITRON-class comparison this row names.
- *Wider synthesis:* **untouched, sharpened.** RESOLVE makes the hypothesis "agents can optimize aggressively when they can rigorously check their results" testable at a measured price; it does not test it.
- *Coordinated optimization:* **untouched.** RESOLVE's megakernel audit found arrival-order dependences in three whole-step systems; that is a correctness finding about the integrated direction, not a performance comparison.
- *Compiler co-evolution:* **untouched.** No generated compiler component this week.
- *Controller improvement:* **untouched.** ATTUNE's "catalog of lessons from past campaigns" is memory adaptation without a held-out controller comparison.
- *Advantage grows with coupling:* **untouched.**
- *Wide adoption:* **untouched, one more organization's production report pending full text.** Meta plus KernelEvolve is one organization; AMD's Hyperloom is another; the row needs independent organizations *and* a disclosed agent share.

**§5.5 predicates.** 2027: **tally 0 of 2**; Meta's report is entered as the first candidate with an application denominator and marked not qualifying (agent share not isolated, directly-ported comparator, body unread). 2029, 2031, both 2036 predicates, 2039 precursor: untouched. **§5.8.3:** all five checkpoints untouched; both September 2027 checkpoints untouched. The "Increase autonomy" row's reason-to-revisit ("evaluation gaps allow the optimizer to improve its score without improving the intended workload") now has two concrete instruments — RESOLVE and HPCAgent-Bench's hidden-seed judge — but the row's threshold is unchanged. **§6:** compiler-specific validation gains its strongest instrument yet but stays open (proof over reals, bitwise links by test, 14 full-pipeline cases); the reuse question gains two anchoring costs (143 min per verified kernel; a recipe campaign repaid within a day); every other question untouched.

**Direction / timing / architecture confidence: unchanged.**

**Strongest objection to my reading.** That I am counting RESOLVE's cost as a ceiling when it is a first implementation: specification and proof dominate the 143 minutes, both are agent-written, and both will get cheaper as models and Kuiper coverage improve, so "proof-level acceptance belongs offline" may be a 2026 statement that the 2027 review overturns. A second objection: three of the four digests rest on abstracts and repositories because arXiv full-text fetches were rate-limited all run; if the Meta body isolates the agent contribution with a strong comparator, the 2027 tally entry should be re-scored, and if HPCAgent-Bench's two significant interventions are large, "harness engineering buys cost, not speed" is overstated.

**Experiment that would settle it.** Take the accepted candidates of one published agent speedup study (a D2K-Bench or KernelBench-X leaderboard), run RESOLVE over all of them, and report three numbers: the fraction that verify, the fraction rejected, and the geometric-mean speedup among verified kernels only. If the verified-only speedup stays near the reported one, the checker gap is a nuisance; if it collapses toward 1×, the agent-side headroom in the register is partly an artifact of the oracle, and the first §5.3 row moves toward "weaken."
